We were walking home through San Francisco after midnight, four of us strung along the sidewalk in various states of exhaustion and theatricality. The fog had softened the streetlights, and every parked car shone as if it had been dipped in mercury. We were discussing something urgent—whether a bartender’s mustache was ironic or merely unfortunate—when a pickup truck slowed beside us.

A man leaned out of the passenger window and shouted a slur. Then something came flying toward us. It struck a parking meter with a metallic crack and dropped harmlessly to the pavement.

For a moment, nobody moved.

“That,” Julian said at last, staring after the truck, “was a terrible review of my outfit.”

The pickup sped away, its engine roaring with all the dignity of a lawn mower falling down a staircase. Someone in the back yelled another insult, but the words dissolved into traffic noise. They had wanted the scene to end with us frightened and silent. Instead, Mara stepped into the street, raised one hand like a disappointed schoolteacher, and shouted, “Your aim is as bad as your politics!”

We laughed—not because the attack was harmless, or because we had not been afraid, but because the alternative was to let those men dictate the meaning of the moment. Their performance depended on appearing powerful: four people sealed inside a moving vehicle, attacking strangers from a safe distance and fleeing before anyone could answer. Seen clearly, it was less a display of strength than a confession of cowardice.

Still, we checked one another carefully. Was anyone hurt? Had anyone been hit? Beneath the jokes ran a current of anger and alarm. We knew how easily the object could have struck a face instead of a parking meter. We knew that queer people had learned to make such calculations automatically—how close the car was, whether the street was crowded, where the nearest open business might be. Humor did not erase that knowledge. It simply kept fear from having the last word.

Julian picked up the object, inspected it, and declared it “evidence of heterosexual decline.” Mara suggested we mail it back with a note about proper throwing technique. I proposed that we leave it where it lay, since even the city’s litter deserved better company.

Then we continued walking.

At the next corner, we passed a bar spilling music and warm light onto the sidewalk. Two men stood outside arguing affectionately about whose turn it was to buy cigarettes. A woman in silver boots waved to someone across the street. Inside, people danced beneath paper stars, crowded together in the ordinary, extravagant business of being alive.

We went in.

Within minutes, Julian was retelling the incident with increasingly elaborate embellishments. By the third version, the attackers were wearing matching camouflage tuxedos. By the fourth, their truck had stalled at a red light and needed to be pushed out of the intersection. Each retelling reduced them further, stripping away the menace they had tried to create until they became what they had always been: ridiculous men mistaking cruelty for courage.

The night did not become innocent again. None of us forgot the sound of the object striking metal or the sudden tightening in our chests. But we refused to surrender the city, the sidewalk, or our pleasure in one another. We ordered drinks, resumed the debate about the bartender’s mustache, and danced until closing.

The men in the truck had wanted us to feel that we did not belong. Our answer was not heroic in any grand sense. We simply stayed together and carried on—laughing, flirting, arguing, occupying space. Yet that ordinary return to queer life was its own form of defiance. They had driven away shouting because they needed us to be afraid. We remained, and in remaining, made them small.

### The Rusty Queer

At the edge of town stood an old bar called **The Rusty Queer**. Its sign creaked in the wind, its letters faded but unapologetically bright. Inside, mismatched chairs surrounded a tiny stage where poets, musicians, and drag performers shared stories that had nowhere else to go.

The place was imperfect—scratched, weathered, and stubbornly alive. Like the people who gathered there, it wore its history openly. Every patch of rust seemed to say that age and hardship did not erase beauty; they gave it character.

For many, The Rusty Queer was more than a bar. It was a refuge, a community, and proof that even forgotten places could become homes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person literary vignette about a gay couple in San Francisco responding to a homophobic drive-by incident with dark humor, camp, and vivid details.
counterfactuals.output:
The car was a dented silver Civic with one jaundiced headlight, which offended Mateo almost as much as the slur.

It came crawling past us on 18th, near Dolores, while we were carrying a lemon tart home from Tartine like two minor saints in a Renaissance painting. Someone in the passenger seat leaned out and shouted the word—long, ugly, and ancient—then the Civic coughed blue smoke and fled downhill.

Mateo watched it go.

“Imagine committing a hate crime in that vehicle,” he said. “The upholstery alone is a cry for help.”

I laughed too loudly. The laugh came out lacquered and brittle, a drag queen’s fingernail tapping a coffin lid.

Around us, San Francisco continued performing innocence. Eucalyptus shivered in the park. A shirtless man glided past on roller skates, trailing gold lamé. The sky had gone the improbable pink of supermarket salmon. Somewhere, a bell rang; somewhere else, a dog in a cashmere sweater was being congratulated for urinating.

“You okay?” I asked.

“Devastated,” Mateo said. “They didn’t even slow down enough to admire my coat.”

It was a green trench he’d bought secondhand in the Haight, dramatic at the shoulders, cinched at the waist. He turned beneath a streetlamp and gave me a wounded runway pivot.

“Thoughts?”

“Widow of a wealthy poisoner.”

“Thank God.”

We kept walking. I held the tart flat between my palms. My fingers had begun to shake, making the glazed raspberries tremble in their neat little congregation. Mateo noticed and slipped his hand beneath the cardboard box, steadying it with me.

There it was: the thing under the joke. The dark animal that had woken in both of us. It knew license plates, emergency rooms, headlines. It knew how quickly a word could become a bottle, a fist, a gun. It had been fed by history and still had excellent teeth.

Mateo leaned his head against mine.

“If they’d ruined this tart,” he said softly, “I would have become a heterosexual’s idea of a homosexual: vengeful, supernatural, and dressed for court.”

“Like Maleficent with a restraining order?”

“Exactly.”

At our apartment, the fog was pushing over Twin Peaks, a slow white curtain closing on the city’s glittering set. We lit every candle we owned—the Diptyque, the Sacred Heart, the one shaped like Dolly Parton—and ate the tart directly from its box.

Mateo raised his fork.

“To surviving men with poor diction and worse credit.”

“To us,” I said.

Outside, an engine backfired. We both flinched.

Then Mateo, with impeccable timing, clutched his pearls—though he wasn’t wearing any—and collapsed across the velvet sofa.

“Tell my mother,” he gasped, “I died as I lived.”

“Overreacting?”

“Moisturized.”

I laughed until I cried, and then kept going because the two had become indistinguishable. Mateo pulled me against him, his mouth bright with lemon curd, his green coat still on, magnificent and ridiculous.

Below our window, the city climbed its impossible hills, all headlights and sirens, sequins and broken glass. It had never promised to love us. Still, night after night, we lit candles in it. We fed each other sweetness. We made a home loud enough to answer back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented memoir passage in which someone throws a hot dog while shouting “QUEER,” but the narrator and their friends mock the attackers and continue their evening.
counterfactuals.output:
The hot dog arrived before the word did.

A pale, mustard-striped comet—  
then the shout from the passing car:

“QUEER!”

The bun struck Milo’s shoulder and fell apart on the pavement. For one stunned second, we stared at it.

Then Lena bowed toward the taillights. “Thank you,” she called, “but we’ve already eaten.”

Milo inspected the mustard on his jacket. “Cowards,” he said. “Not even grilled.”

We laughed—too loudly, maybe, but deliberately. We made a ceremony of it: photographed the wreckage, rated the throw a three out of ten, deducted points for presentation. Someone suggested we frame the bun.

Afterward, the evening kept going.

That is what I remember most. Not the car, not the voice, not the small violence dressed up as a joke.

We kept going.

Into the bar with the sticky floor. Into the blue light and bad music. Into another round, Lena’s hand in mine, Milo dancing in his stained jacket as if mustard were a medal.

Outside, the city continued trying to name us.

Inside, we answered only to each other.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the aftermath of a minor gaybashing near Annie’s Social Club, incorporating an antique-kimono scarf, Woolite, an ATM inside a sex shop, Astrud Gilberto, and colorful dildos.
counterfactuals.output:
Outside Annie’s Social Club, the aftermath looked almost ordinary: a bent pair of glasses, one split lip, two shaken men insisting they were fine. The attackers had already vanished, leaving behind only a slur hanging in the cold air.

Inside, a bartender dabbed blood from an antique-kimono scarf and promised Woolite would save the silk. Someone went next door for cash, using the ATM inside a sex shop, where Astrud Gilberto drifted softly from ceiling speakers above rows of colorful dildos. The absurd tenderness of it all—the bossa nova, the concerned clerk, the scarf soaking in a sink—steadied them.

By closing time, the glasses were taped, the police report filed, and nobody was laughing off what had happened. Still, they walked home together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an edgy queer prose-poem that contrasts everyday adult worries like insurance and interest rates with absurd homophobic harassment from people in an F-150.
counterfactuals.output:
I am thirty-four and afraid of variable interest rates,  
of the dentist saying *crown*,  
of the little spinning wheel on the insurance portal  
deciding whether my body is medically necessary.

Meanwhile, at the red light, an F-150  
the color of a bruised flag  
pulls up beside me.

Four men lean out like gargoyles with truck payments,  
screaming that my shorts have doomed civilization,  
that my iced coffee is an affront to God,  
that somewhere a bald eagle has filed a complaint.

I want to tell them: boys, please.  
I have compared deductibles.  
I have watched love become a shared calendar  
full of oil changes, Pap smears, and *call your mother*.  
You cannot frighten me with hell.  
I have been on hold with Blue Cross.

They rev six hundred horses  
to escape the dangerous sight  
of me holding my boyfriend’s hand.

We stand there—two queers, one reusable tote,  
a sack of avocados ripening faster than our savings—  
while the truck fishtails toward the horizon,  
dragging its thunderous little masculinity behind it  
like cans tied to a wedding car.

The light turns green.

We go home to calculate the mortgage,  
kiss in the kitchen,  
and commit the radical act  
of worrying about tomorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a gritty yet humorous San Francisco scene narrated in a conversational, stream-of-consciousness style, ending with surreal imagery of hot dogs, penguins, and sex toys in many colors and materials.
counterfactuals.output:
The fog came in like it owed somebody money, shoving past the buildings, dampening cigarettes, softening the edges of everything except the rent.

I was walking down Market with one wet sock and half a burrito, which in San Francisco is practically business casual, when a guy in a sequined captain’s hat tried to sell me a parking meter. Not a parking space. The meter itself. He slapped its metal head affectionately and said, “Still takes quarters,” like that was a moral virtue.

A bus sighed at the curb. Nobody got off. Nobody got on. The driver stared straight ahead with the thousand-yard gaze of a person who had seen someone clip their toenails in the priority seats.

Across the street, a tech billboard promised to disrupt loneliness. Beneath it, three actual lonely people shared a cigarette under a torn blue tarp while a tiny dog in a cashmere sweater screamed at a pigeon. The pigeon, hardened by city life, did not even blink.

I kept moving uphill because every direction in this town is uphill, even toward the water, even spiritually. My burrito leaked orange grease onto my jacket. A cable car clanged somewhere in the fog, cheerful as a haunted toaster. From an open window came jazz, then an argument, then jazz again, possibly the same song.

At Sixth, a man with a shopping cart full of mannequin legs asked if I believed in reincarnation.

“On weekdays,” I said.

“Coward,” he replied.

Fair.

By the time I reached the corner, the city had begun to wobble. The Transamerica Pyramid bent down to sip from a puddle. The streetlights sprouted feathers. Sewer steam curled into cursive and spelled out a phone number I almost recognized.

Then the crosswalk filled with hot dogs marching upright in tiny gold boots, followed by solemn penguins carrying briefcases and sex toys in every color and material imaginable—ruby silicone, chrome steel, purple glass, polished wood, translucent pink rubber—all bobbing through the fog like a deeply inappropriate parade, while the little white WALK sign raised both glowing hands and applauded.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
